A page fetch returns old copies of those pages, and a direct request to volcano.si.edu was refused (403). Langila (2026-11-21): first record page of a volcano that never had an old profile (D-63, D-65); type “Complex”, 1,330 m, basalt / picro-basalt, as in the download. The list of all profiles, the profile counts, the map and the search take a page that has no old profile from this file (country, type, elevation, coordinates, year of the last known eruption) and from the eruption file (“2015–present” while the eruption is listed as continuing): `getVolcanoList()` in `lib/data.ts`. Chimborazo (2026-11-21): the reader’s copy of volcano.cfm?vn=352071 is an old one (elevation 6310 m, 1.464°S 78.815°W); the search engine’s copy at the same address prints 6,261 m (20,541 ft) and 1.469°S, 78.817°W, as the download does, and the population figures the page uses (442 within 5 km, 7,561 within 10 km, 463,426 within 30 km, 2,325,666 within 100 km), which the reader’s copy shows as labels without numbers. The Geological Summary reads the same in both copies. It dates the sector collapse to about 35,000 years ago; the Instituto Geofísico and Samaniego and others (2012) to 60–65 thousand years: the page gives the study’s age and names the Smithsonian’s. The page prints the Instituto Geofísico’s summit, 6,263 m, and names the Smithsonian’s. Galeras (2026-11-21): the reader gives the first 100,000 of the 655,539 characters of volcano.cfm?vn=351080: the header facts, the Geological Summary (in the page’s description), the weekly reports of 2004 to 2013 and the newest bulletin (BGVN 43:01, January 2018: ash plumes May 2012 to January 2014, steam emissions through 2017). The population figures (705 within 5 km, 120,817 within 10 km, 630,777 within 30 km, 1,700,248 within 100 km) were read only in the search engine’s copy of the page; the Galeras page prints the 10 km and 30 km figures rounded to the nearest thousand and says where they come from. Bamus (2026-11-21): the reader’s copy of volcano.cfm?vn=252110 has the eruption list, the synonyms (South Son, Sudsohn) and the reports of February and March 1990 and of 12 July 2006, but no header facts and no Geological Summary; those were read in the search engine’s copy of the page and of its placemark text (SW of Ulawun; the two highest volcanoes of the 1,000-km Bismarck arc; rainforest; a breached summit crater filled with a lava dome; a cone on the south flank; a 1.5-km crater with two small cones halfway up the SE flank; young pyroclastic-flow deposits; residents describe an eruption in the late 19th century). One list page of the Smithsonian prints VEI 2 for all four eruptions; the download and the volcano’s own page have VEI 3 with a question mark for 1886 and none for the others, and the page follows the download. Pagan (2026-11-21): the reader’s copy of volcano.cfm?vn=284170 covers the first 100,000 of the page’s 105,494 characters and was read twice with pointed questions. Taken from its bulletin reports: 15 May 1981 (the radio message at 09:15, then contact lost; all 53 persons taken off early on 16 May by the Japanese merchant ship Hoyo Maru; one minor injury; a lava flow to the SW over part of the airstrip, stopped before the village; much arable land covered, livestock killed or starved; radar in Japan put the cloud at 18–20 km); December 2006 (residents at a camp about 3 km SW of the summit told HVO and EMO scientists of ashfall, up to a centimeter a day); May 2010 (trace ash on the tents of a U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service research crew); a later bulletin’s statement that the island remains uninhabited since May 1981, with residents and officials visiting; September 2021 (ash deposits in and around the crater and downwind). The Smithsonian’s separate page for the 1981 bulletin (showreport, SEAN 06:04) answered client_error again and was not retried; lava-flow lengths in the reader’s copy contradict each other (longest 2.8 km, a lobe 3.5 km) and are not printed. Blup Blup (2026-11-21): the reader’s copy of volcano.cfm?vn=251001 has the header (402 m / 1,319 ft; last known eruption “Unknown - Evidence Credible”), no confirmed eruptive period, two entries [1830] and [1616] each marked “Discredited” with no explanation, no bulletin and no weekly report, and one photo caption (a 3.5-km-wide forested island with lava flows with well-defined flow fronts, a weak thermal area on the W coast, no historical eruptions, part of the Schouten Islands with Kadovar and Bam); it has no Geological Summary and no synonyms. The summary printed on the page (2 x 3.5 km; weak thermal areas on the W and N coasts; summit crater about 800 m; a possible lava dome on a ridge to the W and satellite cone on the SW coast; the reports of 1616 and 1830 erroneous, possible Holocene eruptions after “Johnson, 1990 p.c.”; blocks from a submarine debris avalanche to the NE) is the one in the site’s own copy of the Smithsonian’s download (volcanoes.json), the same words as in the search engine’s copy of the Smithsonian’s pages. Synonyms seen only as search text (Garnot Island, Ruprup) are not printed. The Smithsonian’s page for Kadovar (volcano.cfm?vn=251002, reader’s copy) was read for every passage that names Blup Blup: the reports of Nov 1976 and Dec 1976–Feb 1977 (R. Cooke, Rabaul Volcano Observatory: all Kadovar residents evacuated to Blupblup, 13 km north; an observation post expected there; a few men stayed on Kadovar), January 2018 (the whole population to Blup Blup by boats and canoes; about 500 / about 600 / 591; observers there saw incandescence on 12–13 Jan; moved on to the mainland), 9 Feb 2018 (5–6 minor tsunamis under 1 m on Blup Blup’s E and W coasts at about 10:50), Feb and Sep 2018 (sulfur odor, minor ashfall), Jan–Feb 2020 (rumbling, night glow). Its distances differ (10, 13, 15 km): the page prints 13 to 15 km and names the 10 km in its notes. Pululahua (read 2026-11-21): the reader’s copy of volcano.cfm?vn=352011 has header, summary, the four eruptions with the Smithsonian’s own marks (“0290 (?)”, “0450 BCE ± 150 years”, “0690 BCE ± 150 years”, “4800 BCE (?)”), the synonym Pululagua and no weekly or bulletin report. Its photo captions (1978) differ from its summary (caldera floor 3 km wide against a 5-km caldera; 27 km from Quito against 15; caldera formed about 2,400 years ago during the latest dated eruption against a latest eruption about 1,670 years ago): the page prints the summary and names the other sizes with their sources. The page’s population figures are the same for 5 and 10 km and are not printed. Nabro (read three times 2026-11-21): the reader’s copy of volcano.cfm?vn=221101 has no header and no Geological Summary (the summary printed is the one in the site’s own download); it has six weekly reports (8–14 June to 28 Sep–4 Oct 2011), Bulletins 36:09 and 39:05, the eruption row, an emission entry (Aura OMI, 13 June 2011, 18 km, 3,650 kt of SO2: not printed, the page gives the 4.5 Tg of the 2023 study) and the synonym Nabbeo. Bulletin 36:09: the eruption “killed seven people, according to the Eritrean government”, and “later reports appeared to discount that” (no detail): the page says both. Clock times in the weekly report of 8–14 June are not printed (their zone is unclear and a witness time is inconsistent). The photo caption’s 10-km caldera is not used (summary: 8 and 5 km). Suwanosejima (2026-11-21): the reader’s copy of volcano.cfm?vn=282030 served ANOTHER volcano’s page (Nabro, fetched earlier in the session) on two tries more than 15 minutes apart, so nothing was taken from it: the summary printed is the one in the site’s own download (8-km island; two summit craters; the collapse scar open to the east; 1813–14 the largest recorded eruption, the island uninhabited for about 70 years; lava to the east coast in 1884; about 50 residents). Always ask the reader first which volcano the page is about. Purace (2026-11-22): the reader confirmed the page is Puracé’s before anything was taken. Summary from the site’s download (a 600-m summit crater at the NW end of the Los Coconucos chain; nine composite and five monogenetic volcanoes, more than 6 km SE to Pan de Azúcar; largest eruptions 1849, 1869, 1885). From the page: 28–30 Mar 2022 (479 VT, 183 LP and 119 tremor events on the 28th; two fractures about 40 m long between Puracé and Curiquinga with gas and ash; Yellow on the 30th); the 1977 entry reports no casualties or damage. The reports the reader could reach end in 2023. Nevado del Ruiz (2026-11-22): the reader’s copy of volcano.cfm?vn=351020 was SAKURAJIMA’s page, so nothing was taken from it; the summary printed is the site’s download (broad glacier-covered volcano over more than 200 km2; three edifices since the start of the Pleistocene; the modern cone a cluster of lava domes in the caldera of an older one; Arenas crater 1 km wide and 240 m deep; historical eruptions since the 16th century; melting of the ice cap and devastating lahars, the one of 1985 South America’s deadliest eruption). The page says so in its notes. Kirishima (/volcano/kirishimayama, 2026-11-22): the record only (type Shield, 1,700 m, the same height as Japan's weather agency gives Karakunidake); the Smithsonian's page was not fetched and no summary sentence is printed. La Palma (2026-11-22): the record only (Stratovolcano(es), 2,426 m = IGN's Roque de los Muchachos; the coordinates 28.57N 17.83W are on Cumbre Vieja, not at the summit); no summary sentence printed. Sabancaya (2026-11-22): the record (Stratovolcano(es), 5,960 m, andesite to basaltic andesite, 15.787S 71.857W); the volcano page's copy is old (newest weekly narrative July 2024) but gives: NE of Ampato and SE of Hualca Hualca, Holocene Plinian eruptions and lava flows forming an apron on all sides but the south, activity from 1986 the first recorded since 1784, cones table Ampato 6,278 m and Hualca Hualca 5,978 m.

sample_note: Fields: eruption number, confirmed or uncertain, VEI, start and end dates with modifiers and uncertainty, dating method, activity area. notes: The terms ask for the Smithsonian's written permission before commercial use (ads). The owner decided on 2026-11-16 not to request it, so ads on pages built on this data are his accepted risk. Use is kept narrow: facts and numbers in the site's own words with a link to the record, no copied text on rebuilt pages, no Smithsonian photos. The site carries no ads today. Cite as "Global Volcanism Program, Smithsonian Institution" with version and date. The DOI printed for v. 5.4 did not resolve on 2026-11-15, so link the volcano page instead. Date limits (D-65, 2026-11-21): the eruption layer’s “<” and “>” on a start or end are the Smithsonian’s “in or before” / “on or before” and “on or after”. Read on its own pages as the search engine shows them: Stromboli “1558 (in or before)” (volcano.cfm?vn=211040&vtab=Eruptions, volcanolist_countries.cfm?country=Italy), Langila “2009 Sep 16 (on or before) ± 15 days” and “2000 Oct 16 (on or after) ± 15 days” (volcanolist_countries.cfm?country=Papua_New_Guinea, faq/Longest_Eruptions.cfm). The tables print them as “(or earlier)” and “(or later)” with a sentence under the table; 51 date cells on the 20 rebuilt pages that were live carry such a mark, and two on Langila’s. Langila: 30 rows, 26 confirmed; the first five (1878, 1884, 1890, 1900, 1907) carry a year only; the Smithsonian’s note on the 1878 row (first recorded eruption put at 1878, 1880, 1884 or 1900; Cooke 1976 preferred 1878; Palfreyman 1981 took the early descriptions to be of older lava flows) was read in the reader’s copy of its Langila page (three readings). A length or a gap that a table works out from a date with such a limit says “at least” or “at most” (on 2026-11-21: rows on the pages of Langila, Manam, Nyiragongo, Pinatubo, Shishaldin and Stromboli); where two limits pull in opposite directions the table says neither. Chimborazo (D-66, 2026-11-21): six rows, every one a year with a margin (75 to 2,500 years), no end, no VEI, dated by tephrochronology (3) or calibrated radiocarbon (3). A last eruption given as a year with a margin is printed as “about 550 CE”, with the margin, and counted in round terms (this year minus the year, rounded to the nearest 100 years for a margin of 50 to 499 years, to 10 below that, to 1,000 above); the calculation is printed on the page. The record table now writes a margin with a thousands separator (“± 2,500 years”), which changes cells on the pages of Sakurajima, Mount Asama, Mount Erebus, Hekla and Mount Pelee. Galeras (2026-11-21): 42 rows, 36 confirmed (30 from reports, 5 by calibrated radiocarbon, 1 by tephrochronology); the end of the last eruption (30 Jan 2014) carries a margin of one day and prints as “about January 30, 2014”; one row runs from 1670 to 1736; three ratings carry a question mark (1974, 2002, 2007) and two a “^” (1535, 1616), which the table does not print; six rows are not confirmed (1836, 1930, 1933, 1947, 1973, 2011). Bamus (2026-11-21): four rows, none with an end; the newest is the Smithsonian’s “1886 Jul 2 ± 8 years ± 182 days”: a placeholder month and day of year-only precision and a margin on the year. Such a last eruption is now treated like Chimborazo’s (D-66): “about 1886”, counted in round terms (140 years, rounded to 10). The record table now keeps the year’s margin on such rows (“1886 ± 8 years”); 81 rows of the database have both marks, two of them in tables of live pages: Colima (“1926 ± 4 years”, was “1926”) and Manam (“1899 ± 1 year”, was “1899”). Pagan (2026-11-21): 24 rows, 21 confirmed (19 from reports, two radiocarbon; three unconfirmed: 1929–30 at South Pagan, February 1988, April 2009). The list dates the last eruption 29 Jul – 6 Sep 2021 (39 days); USGS’s notices date the eruption itself from 1 September, the first day of ash, and the page says so beside the list’s dates. One confirmed row (1864) is placed at South Pagan; none between 1925 and 1981; the 1981 row is open to “1985 May 1 or later”. The strip starts in 1650 and its caption names the one older entry (1340 ± 100). Blup Blup (2026-11-21): no row at all, confirmed or uncertain; the first record page for a volcano with no eruption on the list (D-68): the headline number is the count itself (0), the strip is a flat line with the two discredited reports as crossed-out marks (typed in the profile from the Smithsonian’s page and summary: they are not in the download), key facts read “Last eruption: Unknown”, and the page has no eruption tables. Pululahua (2026-11-21): four rows, all confirmed and radiocarbon (uncalibrated), none with an end; the first and the last carry a question mark on the year and no margin. Such a last eruption (“0290 ?”) had no rule: it now prints as “about 290 CE (date uncertain)” and is counted to the nearest 100 years (D-66, point 6). Ecuador’s Instituto Geofísico dates the last eruption about 2,200 years before the present: the page gives both in its headline and answer. The Smithsonian’s data service was asked directly for the four rows the same day (the margins of 150 years are there). Nabro (2026-11-21): one row, 2011 Jun 13 to 2012 Jun 3 with a question mark on the end day, VEI 4. Bulletin 39:05 gives 3 June 2012 as the day of the last satellite heat alert; the studies date the start to 12 June (20:27–20:45 UTC). The page prints the list’s dates and says where the two ends come from. First record page with exactly one eruption: the template’s “Show all N eruptions” now reads “Show the one eruption”. Suwanosejima (2026-11-21): 27 rows, 24 confirmed; the current eruption from 2004 Oct 23, continuing at the list’s last update (2026 Nov 6); four eruptions rated VEI 4 (about 1600, 1813, 1877 with a question mark, 1889); the longest entry 1956 to 1984. Purace (2026-11-22): 29 rows, all confirmed (28 from reports, one by radiocarbon about 160 BCE); the current eruption from 2025 Nov 23, continuing at the last update (2026 Nov 9); three rated VEI 3 (1847–52 and 1869 with a question mark, 1885 without); nothing between Mar 1977 and Mar 2022; the entry of 2025 Jan 19 is at the Curiquinga crater (the survey dates that event 20 Jan). Nevado del Ruiz (2026-11-22): 24 rows, 20 confirmed (13 reported, 5 radiocarbon, 2 tephrochronology); the last eruption 2014 Nov 18 to 2026 Mar 8 (VEI 2, Arenas crater), so the volcano is NOT erupting by the list; 1985 Sep 11 to 1991 Jul 13 (VEI 3); 2012 Feb 22 to 2013 Jul 12 (VEI 3); four rated VEI 4, the most recent 1595 (Mar 9). Kirishima (2026-11-22): 85 rows, 79 confirmed (70 reported, 3 radiocarbon, 6 tephrochronology), 6 unconfirmed; the last eruption 2025 Jun 22 to Sep 7 (VEI 3, no area given; JMA: Shinmoedake), so NOT erupting by the list; 2018 Mar 1 to about Jun 22 (JMA's last eruption that year: Jun 27); four VEI 4, the latest 1235 (Ohachi); no row for Ioyama's eruptions of 19 and 26 Apr 2018, which JMA records. The page says both. La Palma (2026-11-22): 14 rows, all confirmed (8 reported, 4 radiocarbon, 2 K/Ar); the last 2021 Sep 19 to Dec 13 (VEI 3, 'Tajogaite eruption'), NOT erupting; the list's dates give about 3 months, the Canary government and IGN 85 days 8 hours (table.last_length); 1481 +/- 11 years for Tacande while IGN names 1430; the page says both. Sabancaya (2026-11-22): 15 rows, 12 confirmed (9 reported, 2 tephrochronology, 1 radiocarbon); ERUPTING: 2025 Sep 13 continuing (last update 2026 Nov 8, VEI 3), before it 2016 Nov 6 to 2025 Apr 6 (VEI 3, Sabancaya crater); count_from 1986 (7 since); IGP counts the two as one process since 6 Nov 2016 and counts 5 eruptions since 1750 (calc note).

sample_note: One item per volcano: name, country, report period, text, coordinates, publication date. Pages must print the report period and warn when the feed is stale.
notes: The terms ask for the Smithsonian's written permission before commercial use (ads). The owner decided on 2026-11-16 not to request it, so ads on pages built on this data are his accepted risk. Use is kept narrow: facts and numbers in the site's own words with a link to the record, no copied text on rebuilt pages, no Smithsonian photos. The site carries no ads today. Cite as "Global Volcanism Program, Smithsonian Institution" with version and date. The DOI printed for v. 5.4 did not resolve on 2026-11-15, so link the volcano page instead. Rebuilt pages take only the week, the entry's heading and its link from the feed (lib/weekly.ts). The Kanlaon page (2026-11-17) also quotes the weekly reports of June to December 2024 as shown on the Smithsonian’s page for the volcano (explosions of 3 Jun and 9 Dec 2024, gas records, evacuation counts relayed from PHIVOLCS, NDRRMC and DROMIC) and the Bulletin of the Global Volcanism Network 21:07 for the explosion of 10 Aug 1996. The Bulusan page (2026-11-17) quotes the weekly report for 23–29 Apr 2025 (its own page) and, from the Smithsonian’s page for the volcano, the report for 14–20 May 2026 (as shown in search results), the reports on the eruptions of June 2022 and one death in 2006, and the danger-zone radii; the crater size is from the Bulletin of the Global Volcanism Network, September 2006. The Ambae page (2026-11-17) quotes, as shown in search results, the Bulletin of the Global Volcanism Network 43:02, 43:07 and 44:02, the weekly report for 4–10 Apr 2018, and weekly reports of August and September 2018 on the Smithsonian’s page for the volcano (evacuation of all 10,000 residents by 14 Aug 2018, relayed from Radio New Zealand; alert lowered to 2 on 21 Sep 2018). The Nyiragongo page (2026-11-17) rests on pages fetched and read that day: the Bulletin of the Global Volcanism Network 46:06 (May 2021 eruption, geological summary) and 27:03 (January 2002), the weekly report issue for 19–25 May 2021 (reports_weekly.cfm?weekstart=20210519), the Smithsonian’s page for the volcano (weekly reports of 2002, 2021, 2023 and 2024, the March 1977 report) and its Current Eruptions page (eruption type “Lava Lake”; continuing = no break of three months or more). Three other report addresses returned an error to the reader and are not cited. Found the same day: the Smithsonian’s RSS feed of the weekly report stopped on 15 Oct 2026 while its site carries reports to 5–11 Nov 2026; record pages now say “Weekly report of <week>” and name the feed’s date instead of calling a stale entry the latest. The Colima page (2026-11-17) rests on pages fetched and read that day: the Bulletin of the Global Volcanism Network 44:08 (the 2019 eruption, geological summary), the weekly report issue for 8–14 July 2015 (reports_weekly.cfm?weekstart=20150708) and the weekly reports on the Smithsonian’s page for the volcano (2016, 2017, 2019, October 2023). Krakatoa (2026-11-21): the Smithsonian’s Krakatau page reaches the reader only as an old copy (nothing after 2023) and the page’s Weekly tab fails for the reader, so the weekly reports of 8–14 October, 15–21 October and 29 October–4 November 2026 were read as the search engine shows them at the page’s own addresses (volcano.cfm?vn=262000 and its Weekly tab): level raised to 3 of 4 at 21:00 on 9 October with a 5 km distance; 1 km from the small islands to the NW and SE; plumes to 500 m on 29 October and to 200 m on 2–3 November; level still 3 in the newest of them. The old copy was used for the bulletin text on 2018–2023, the photo captions and the feature table (Rakata 813 m). Langila (2026-11-21): the reader’s copy of volcano.cfm?vn=252010 stops at the weekly report of 12–18 March 2025, and a weekly report page of its own (showreport.cfm?gvpvar=GVP.WVAR20241023-252010), a bulletin page (showreport.cfm?doi=…SEAN198101-252010) and the placemark file answered client_error. The weekly reports of 2026 (7–13 May, 18–24 June, 23–29 July, the plume of 24 August, 17–23 September, 22–28 October; all Darwin VAAC, satellite images) were therefore taken word for word from the search engine’s copy of the page at its own address, as for Krakatoa; the copy’s index also lists February 2026, not read, and the page says so. The page prints only what those sentences say. The bulletins (CSLP 96-73 of July 1973 to BGVN 48:11 of November 2023) were read in the reader’s copy with offsets 0, 100,000, 200,000 and 300,000, each with pointed questions (two readings of the first and last parts): no death, injury or evacuation in any of them except the voluntary evacuation of June 2005. The Geological Summary was read sentence by sentence in the search engine’s copies of four Smithsonian addresses (a showreport page, the placemark file, reports_bgvn.cfm?IssueYear=1990&IssueMonth=10, volcanolist_countries.cfm) and agrees with the reader’s copy of Bulletin 48:11. Galeras (2026-11-21): no entry in the feed. The page’s section on 2004 to 2010 rests on the weekly reports printed on the Smithsonian’s volcano page (read 2026-11-17 and 2026-11-21): ash to 11 km altitude on 17 Jan 2008 and to 12 km on 2 Jan 2010; the alert raised to Level I (then the highest) after the larger explosions; about 8,000 people ordered out on 14 Feb 2009 (few went), about 9,000 on 20 Nov 2009 (900 to 1,000 went to shelters), about 7,000 asked to leave on 25 Aug 2010 (few left). The reports take those numbers from news articles, and the page says so. The report of 12–18 Jul 2006 (about 10,000 ordered out) was seen only in the search engine’s copy and is not printed.

sample_note: Fields: date, volcano, VEI, deaths, injuries, damage, linked tsunami and earthquake records. 480 events record deaths. Deep link per event: event-more-info/<id>. Spot-checked Stromboli (15 events), plus the 1930 event page. Downloaded again on 2026-11-21: the events of every volcano are unchanged since 2026-11-16. Krakatau, read 2026-11-21 through the same service (hazard-service/api/v1/volcanoes/2429/info and /7264/info): event 2429 (27 August 1883: VEI 6; deaths 36,417, of them 2,000 from the eruption itself; comments: an estimated 2,000 killed in southern Sumatra by “hot ashes”; all 3,150 people on the islands between Krakatau and Sumatra killed; 165 villages destroyed and 132 partly; near-source deposits about 12 km3; a column of about 40 km more likely than the 80 km reported; the Smithsonian’s summary, with “the 2nd largest in Indonesia during historical time”); event 7264 (22 December 2018: NOAA’s VEI 4, 437 deaths, 31,943 injuries). Etna, read 2026-11-21 through the same service (events 41, 1, 1350, 6246, 44, 28, 1581, 30, 31, 6264, 1628, 14, 5485, 5487, 6965, 7284 and 4724, each as /<id> and /<id>/info): event 1 (4 February 1169): 16,000 deaths, with the comments “Eruption is uncertain” and an earthquake “(probably tectonic)” that buried people in Catania and a tsunami at Messina; event 1350 (11 March 1669): one account’s 20,000 deaths “seems unlikely”, the standard accounts mention none; event 6246: two killed and five injured by a lava flow on 19 March 1669; event 44 (25 November 1843): 59 deaths at Bronte when the front of the flow blew out, perhaps over a cistern; event 28 (8 November 1928): five deaths at Mascali; event 1581 (1929): two killed by an explosion at the Northeast Crater; event 30 (12 September 1979): nine killed by rocks from the Bocca Nuova; event 31 (17 April 1987): two tourists killed; event 7284 (26 December 2018): 28 injuries, 15 houses destroyed. Event notes read 2026-11-21 through the service (volcanoes/<id>/info) for all 187 events of the live pages, and used on fifteen of them: for example Hekla 1300 (600 dead of a famine in the winter after the ash fall), Santorini 1926 (deaths more likely due to an earthquake than an eruption), Mount St. Helens 1980 (57 deaths from the eruption and 61 in all, the note naming a crop-duster pilot, a traffic death in Yakima and two people who died shoveling ash), Reventador 2002 (an undisclosed number of deaths and injuries among people clearing roofs; Quito’s airport closed for eight days), Fuji 1707 (no victims recorded from the ash fall; many died of starvation afterward).
notes: NOAA counts an eruption as significant if it caused deaths, about $1 million or more in damage, reached VEI 6, caused a tsunami or came with a significant earthquake. Etna: 16,000 of NOAA’s 16,123 deaths are filed under 4 February 1169 and its own comment assigns them to an earthquake, so the page says so wherever the total appears and counts 123 without that entry. Since 2026-11-21 (D-64) the site keeps NOAA’s description of a toll where NOAA has no count (its fields deathsAmountOrder and deathsAmountOrderTotal: few, some, many, very many) and prints it in place of “none”; 128 of the 900 events have a description and no count. The classes and their ranges are NOAA’s own, read on 2026-11-21 on its map legend (gis.ngdc.noaa.gov/arcgis/rest/services/web_mercator/hazards/MapServer/6: “Few Deaths (~1 to 50 people)” to “Very Many Deaths (~1001 or more people)”) and on its poster of March 2024 (ncei.noaa.gov/sites/default/files/2024-05/2023_vol_poster_20240502_a2.pdf), which also says that total deaths include indirect causes such as famine and disease. The count kept is NOAA’s total; two events have a count and no total (Kilauea 1998, Tengger Caldera 2004) and keep their count. The list endpoint carries no comments: a page that says what NOAA’s note tells, or that NOAA tells nothing, must have read volcanoes/<id>/info for that event. Langila (2026-11-21): no event in the database; the page says so. Chimborazo (2026-11-21): no event in the database; the page says so. Galeras (2026-11-21): one event, 4502 (14 Jan 1993, VEI 2, 9 deaths); its comment, read through the info endpoint: “A sudden explosion killed 9 persons, including 6 volcanologists who were in (and on the rim of) the inner crater.” Bamus (2026-11-21): no event in the database; the page says so. Pagan (2026-11-21): no event in the database; the page says so. Blup Blup (2026-11-21): no event in the database; the page says so. Pululahua (2026-11-21): no event in the database; the page says so. Nabro (2026-11-21): event 5524 asked from the hazard service directly (…/volcanoes/5524 and /info): filed under 22 June 2011, VEI 4, 31 deaths, injuries described as many (order 3), damage order 1. Its comment carries both counts: at least seven deaths in Eritrea by a news article (from the Smithsonian’s weekly report) and, from a news report of July 2011, the Afar regional office’s 31 deaths in Bidu woreda, Ethiopia, “as a result of the volcano ash”, with livestock deaths, migration, water shortage, illness and malnutrition in six woredas. The page gives the two counts side by side with who counted what. The news report itself (The New Humanitarian) did not open for the reader: NOAA’s comment is the source cited. Suwanosejima (2026-11-21): no event in the database; the page says so. Purace (2026-11-22, both events read in full through NOAA’s service): 3846, 25 May 1885, VEI 3, no count, deaths coded 2 = “some (about 51 to 100)”, comment: a catastrophic explosion with an earthquake killed many people and destroyed many houses; 3851, 26 May 1949, VEI 2, 17 deaths, comment: university students killed by block ejection as they tried to reach the summit. In the notes the 1885 code was first misread as “few”; the page prints “some”, as the site’s table does. Nevado del Ruiz (2026-11-22, all three events read in full through NOAA’s service): 1595 Mar 12 (the Smithsonian: Mar 9), 636 deaths, lahars in the Lagunillas and Guali valleys, mostly Guali Indians; 1845 Feb 19, 1,000 deaths, mudflows from melted snow buried the population along the Lagunillas valley (linked to NOAA earthquake event 1867); 1985 Nov 13, 23,080 deaths and 10,000 injured, comment: tolls uncertain, most estimates 23,000 to 26,000, the figure from the office of the Colombian President (Perison et al.), Katsui et al. 24,270 including 21,000 of Armero’s 29,000 inhabitants, Naranjo et al. about 1,000 dead in Chinchiná, 5,200 needing medical attention. Kirishima (2026-11-22, all nine events read in full through NOAA's service): 1566 Oct 31 toll described as many (code 3), no count; 1716 Nov 9 and 1717 Feb 7, one death each (note: one source lists 6 for 1716-1717); 1895 Oct 16, 4; 1896 Mar 15, 1 climber killed, 1 injured; 1900 Feb 16, 2 killed, 3 injured; 1923 Jul 1, 1 (JMA lists eruptions on Jul 11, 15, 16 and 20; the page notes the difference); 1989 Aug 26, 2 deaths, note 'No eruption.'; 2011 Jan 28, injuries and damage described, more than 180 window panes broken about 6 km from the crater. La Palma (2026-11-22, all three events read in full): 1677 Nov 22, gas killed one man and many animals; 1971 Oct 28 (Teneguia), toll described as few, 'casualties occurred but very little damage reported'; 2021 Sep 19, 1 death (a 72-year-old man found in an El Paso exclusion zone in Nov 2021; court: toxic gases), damage US$924M, houses destroyed 1,345, the Catastro and Copernicus building counts. Sabancaya (2026-11-22): no event in the database; the page says so.

sample_note: Stromboli: highest point about 926 m, crater terrace at about 700–750 m, base about 2,000 m below sea level, explosions minutes to hours apart, strongest paroxysms 1919, 1930, 2003, 2019, ages of about 200,000 and 85,000 years. Eyjafjallajökull (read 2026-11-17): IMO page: most recent eruption 2010, about 25 km west of Katla, ice-filled caldera about 2.5 km wide; ICAO report: flank eruption 20 Mar–12 Apr 2010, summit eruption from 01:15 on 14 Apr under about 200 m of ice to 22 May (39 days), last activity 17 Jun, plume mostly 4–8 km and never above 10 km, tephra 0.27 km³, about 100,000 flights cancelled, two deaths from exposure, summit 1,651 m at Hámundur, ice cap about 80 km² above 800–900 m. Mount Pinatubo (read 2026-11-17): HazardHunterPH monitoring page: Alert Level 0, “No eruption in foreseeable future”. Cotopaxi (read 2026-11-17): IG-EPN profile: 5,897 m, 45 km SE of Quito and 35 km NE of Latacunga, slopes up to 35°, base about 20 km, crater about 800 by 650 m, five eruptive periods since 1532, eruptions of 2015 and of October 2022 to July 2023, first seismic station 1976, more than 300,000 people in lahar zones. Reports list: newest report 21 Oct 2026, internal and surface activity low and unchanged; no ash emissions since July 2023. 1877 article: pyroclastic flows on 26 Jun 1877 melted part of the glacier; lahars reached Latacunga in a little over 30 minutes, the Chillos Valley in under an hour, the mouth of the Esmeraldas in about 18 hours; ash nearly 2 cm at Machachi, 6 mm in Quito. Sakurajima (read 2026-11-17): JMA catalogue chapter: Kitadake 1,117 m and Minamidake 1,060 m; peninsula 12.2 by 9.5 km on the southern rim of the Aira caldera (17 by 23 km); an island until lava closed the Seto strait on 29 Jan 1914; 1914 eruption from about 10:00 on 12 Jan, M 7.1 earthquake at 18:29, 1.58 km3 of magma, 58 killed and 112 injured, about 2,140 buildings buried or burnt; 1779 eruption 1.86 km3 and over 150 killed; 474 summit explosions in 1985, 994 at the Showa crater in 2011; alert levels since 1 Dec 2007; Kagoshima City 608,219 residents and the Sakurajima area 5,262 (2011). Arenal (read 2026-11-17): RSN profile: about 7 km WSW of La Fortuna, about 1,750 m, about 7,000 years old, eruption from the morning of 29 Jul 1968, three new craters on the west flank, more than 0.5 km3 of lava by 2010, last lava advances reported January 2011, at rest since, 81 deaths in all. RSN paper: 15 km2 laid waste in three days in 1968, 78 killed, 230 km2 affected. OVSICORI bulletin of 18 Oct 2024: 1,755 m, activity level “Calma”. Mount Pelee (read 2026-11-17): OVSM-IPGP bulletin for September 2026 (issued 17 Oct 2026): reactivation since April 2019, degraded vegetation on the south-west flank since late 2019, summit inflation mid-2021 to end-2022 and again from September 2025, 655 volcanic earthquakes in September 2026 (largest Mlv 1.96, none felt), alert level yellow of four (green, yellow, orange, red), short-term probability of an eruption low; phreatic eruptions 1792 and 1851, last magmatic eruption ended 1932, fumaroles stopped 1970. IPGP list of releases: newest weekly report dated 13 Nov 2026, alert yellow. Mount Asama (read 2026-11-17): JMA catalogue chapter 45: 2,568 m, on the Gunma–Nagano border, Kamayama crater about 500 m east–west by 440 m north–south with a depth that changes with each eruption, typical eruptions vulcanian with pyroclastic flows; 1108 eruption 0.62 km3 DRE; 1783 eruption May to August, Agatsuma pyroclastic flow 4 Aug, Kanbara pyroclastic flow and debris avalanche 5 Aug, lahars blocked the “Azuma River” and the water surged into the Tone River, Onioshidashi lava, 1,151 dead, 1,061 houses swept away, 51 burned, over 130 destroyed; “ten and several dozen eruptions” every month in 1941; climbers killed in 1913, 1936, 1947 (nine, by blocks) and 1950; explosive activity resumed 1 Sep 2004 after 21 years, ash that day in Gunma and Fukushima prefectures and on 14–18 Sep in Tokyo and Chiba; 2 Feb 2009 plume 2,000 m, ash in the Kanto region; alert levels since 1 Dec 2007. JMA English page: most active volcano on Honshu, about 140 km NW of Tokyo, all recorded eruptions at the summit, great eruptions 1108 and 1783. JMA status page: Volcanic Alert Level 1, lowered from 2 on 22 May 2026; commentary No. 48 of 13 Nov 2026: volcanic earthquakes up slightly since late September, 36 a day on average over the previous month, plume unchanged, SO2 low, no inflation. Sakurajima status page (read 2026-11-17): warning in force at Volcanic Alert Level 3, issued 27 Jul 2022 20:00 when the level was lowered from 5 after the explosion of 24 Jul 20:05 that threw large blocks more than 2.4 km; commentary No. 102 of 16 Nov 2026 16:00: eruptive activity continues, very small eruptions at times at the Minamidake summit crater, glow at night, no explosions and 4 to 12 volcanic earthquakes a day on 13–16 Nov, no tremor; caution within about 2 km of the Minamidake and Showa craters. Kanlaon (read 2026-11-17): HazardHunterPH: Alert Level 2, probable intrusion of magma at depth, entry into the permanent danger zone prohibited. PHIVOLCS bulletins (text as shown in search results): eruption bulletin 25 Oct 2025: explosion at 8:05 PM on 24 Oct, three minutes, plume 2,000 m; bulletin 27 Feb 2026: explosion at 7:04 PM on 26 Feb, two minutes, SO2 average 2,800 t/day since 3 Jun 2024, edifice inflating since 2022; daily summary 27 Feb 2026: Alert Level 2, 4-km-radius permanent danger zone, provinces of Negros Occidental and Negros Oriental; bulletin 10 Jul 2026: explosion at 7:33 AM on 9 Jul, three minutes, rock fragments up to 30 cm reported within 5 km in Canlaon City. Bulusan (read 2026-11-17): HazardHunterPH: Alert Level 1, disturbances at shallow depth near the crater or around the Irosin caldera, entry into the permanent danger zone prohibited. PHIVOLCS bulletins (text as shown in search results): 28 Apr 2025 07:00 AM: phreatic eruption at 04:36 AM, 24 minutes, plume 4,500 m, ashfall in barangays of Irosin and Juban, alert raised from 0 to 1; eruption update of the same day: 53 volcanic earthquakes on 27 Apr, rumbling about 15 minutes before; 29 Apr 2025 11:00 PM: second phreatic eruption at 07:43 PM, about 77 minutes, up to about 1 cm of ash in parts of Sorsogon Province; March 2026 advisory: swarms often precede Bulusan’s phreatic eruptions; 22 Mar 2026 12:00 PM: alert raised from 0 to 1 after 475 volcanic earthquakes since 15 Mar 2026; eruption-history table: eruptions of 2022 and 2025 classed phreatic. Ambae (read 2026-11-17): VMGD page for Manaro Voui: alert level 3 “Minor Eruption”; most voluminous active shield volcano of the Vanuatu arc; two nested calderas, the larger about 6 km across, three lakes in the smaller (Manaro-Ngoru, Manaro-Lakwa, Manaro-Voui); 1,496 m; eruptions listed: 1995, 2005, 10 Jul 2011, 18–19 Aug 2016, 6 Sep 2017–21 Sep 2018 (largest and most damaging in recent history). VMGD warnings page: warning issued 23 Feb 2026, alert raised to Level 3, activity confined to Lake Voui, Danger Zone B about 3 km around the active vent. VMGD bulletin No. 10 of 31 Oct 2024: Level 2 (major unrest) since 27 Dec 2021, danger zone about 2 km around the 2017–2018 vents. Nyiragongo (2026-11-17): the Goma Volcano Observatory (OVG) was read only as relayed in the Smithsonian’s weekly reports on its page for the volcano (fetched; the tool’s copy ends at July 2024): 22–28 Feb 2023 lava lake still active 13–19 Feb; 20–26 Mar 2024 Alert Level Yellow, CO2 lethal in the “mazuku”, lowland areas in the west of Goma. Colima (2026-11-17), all fetched and read: Mexico’s Servicio Meteorológico Nacional, notice No. 424 of 17 Nov 2026 (the volcano in a stage of passive degassing); Colima state’s civil protection unit (UEPC), notes of 2 Jan 2026 (calm and stable, no explosions) and 10 Jan 2025 (green on its scale, exclusion zone 8 km); the University of Colima’s volcano center (CUEV), its page on the volcano (height 3,860 m, eruptions named, 1913 crater about 500 m deep, pyroclastic flows of July 2015 to 10.3 km, hazards) and the page of weekly bulletin No. 466. Manam (read 2026-11-17): no site of the Rabaul Volcano Observatory was found, so its statements and the Darwin Volcanic Ash Advisory Centre’s observations were read in the Smithsonian’s reports: the weekly feed (8–14 Oct 2026: ash plumes to 2.1 km on 8–9 and 11–13 Oct), the weekly issue of 26 Jan–1 Feb 2005 (the blast of 27 Jan 2005), Bulletin 44:10 (January and June 2019, the Geological Summary) and, on the Smithsonian’s Manam page, the bulletins of 1992, Dec 1996, Nov 2004, Feb 2005 and 2006–2010. Mount Fuji (read 2026-11-18): the Japan Meteorological Agency’s status page data.jma.go.jp/vois/data/report/activity_info/314.html (eruption forecast, Volcanic Alert Level 1; the forecast in force dates from 1 Dec 2007; no information in the past week; newest item the regular commentary for October 2026), its commentary for August 2026 (quiet, no sign of an eruption, no steam at the summit, few volcanic earthquakes, no deformation; seismicity up after the M6.4 earthquake of 15 Mar 2011 and low again since 2016) and the Fujisan chapter of its catalogue, read twice (3,776 m at Kengamine; built over Komitake and Kofuji; about 400 km3; mainly basalt; more than 100 flank eruption sites; 864 Jogan eruption 1.2 km3 DRE; 1707 Hoei eruption 0.7 km3 DRE, VEI 5, about 380 hours, 5 cm of ash at Kawasaki; alert levels since 1 Dec 2007). Hekla (read 2026-11-18): the Icelandic Meteorological Office’s page en.vedur.is/volcanoes/about-volcanoes/hekla/ (central volcano 1490 m, fissure swarm about 60 km, 23 eruptions in historical time, last eruption 2000, third most active, about 100 eruptions in 9,000 years) and its “Hekla eruptions” page (repose time sets the silica of the first magma and the size of the opening phase); its article “Monitoring of Hekla” of 7 Jul 2016, read at en.vedur.is/earthquakes-and-volcanism/articles/monitoring-hekla (decadal eruptions 1970–2000, considered overdue, quiet spells up to 120 years before 1970, plume 10–12 km in 2000 and about 30 km in 1947, warning under an hour at best, tilt past its pre-2000 level between 2007 and 2009, no SO2 since 2014); its hazards page on earthquakes (public warning about half an hour before the 2000 eruption); its report VÍ 2019-003 for ICAO, first 100,000 of 112,018 characters (warning issued 41 minutes before the 2000 eruption; none before 1970, 1980–81, 1991; 23 to 79 minutes from first earthquakes to eruption; best-case alert times; three air routes over Hekla; inflation since 2000); and its list of VONA notifications (35 changes of the aviation colour code from 20 Nov 2024 to 10 Nov 2026, none for Hekla). The Smithsonian’s Hekla page was read whole (90,455 characters) on its host a.cf11.si.edu: general information and the bulletins of 1970, 1980, 1981, 1991, 2000 and 2014 (the seismic unrest of March–April 2013). sample_note: Mauna Loa: summit 4,169 m (13,679 ft), threat potential very high, flanks about 5,000 m further down to the sea floor, sea floor pressed down about 8,000 m, more than 17,000 m base to summit, 34 eruptions since 1843, three since 1950, 38 years quiet from 1984 to 2022, first lava 0.6 to 1 million years ago, above the sea about 300,000 years ago, area about 5,100 km2, volume at least 75,000 km3, caldera 5 by 3.2 km, 2022 flows 19 km long and 2.8 km short of the highway. All five pages answer 200. Mount St. Helens (17 Nov 2026): summit 9,677 ft before and 8,363 ft after May 18, 1980; crater 1.2 by 1.8 miles and 2,084 ft deep; 57 deaths; landslide 0.67 cubic miles; blast 230 square miles; 2004–08 dome about 92 million m3; history about 300,000 years. All three pages answer 200. Kilauea (read 2026-11-17): summit 1,222 m (4,009 ft); eruption since 23 Dec 2024, episode 56 on 5 Nov 2026; tallest fountain 540 m (1,770 ft) in episode 43 on 10 Mar 2026; Halemaʻumaʻu floor 1,023 m before and 518 m after the 2018 collapse, lava surface 1,007 m on 30 Jun 2026; 2018: 35.5 sq km covered, 875 acres of new land, 62 collapses. Mount Pinatubo (read 2026-11-17): Fact Sheet 113-97: more than 1 cubic mile (5 km3) erupted on 15 Jun 1991, ash cloud 22 miles (35 km) high, deposits up to 660 ft (200 m) thick, caldera 1.6 miles (2.5 km) across, nearly 20 million tons of SO2, about 1°F (0.5°C) of cooling 1991–93, at least 5,000 lives and $250 million saved. Fire and Mud: former summit 1,745 m; climactic eruption from 13:42 for about 9 hours; flows 12–16 km; evacuations of about 5,000, then 25,000, then at least 58,000 people; about 14,500 left Clark Air Base on 10 Jun; six earlier eruptive periods, the first more than 35,000 years ago and about five times the size of 1991; caldera more than 650 m deep. 2016 feature: more than 840 deaths, at least 17 jets damaged, about $100 million. Mount Pelee (read 2026-11-17, from the pages’ text in search results): Volcano Watch “Dual volcanic tragedies in the Caribbean led to founding of HVO”: St. Pierre destroyed on 8 May 1902 in 2–3 minutes, 28,000 deaths, a day after Soufrière on St. Vincent (2,000 deaths) 150 km away; FAQ: a pyroclastic flow (“nuée ardente”) killed nearly 30,000; Volcano Watch on Frank Perret: the 1929–32 eruption built a lava dome whose collapses fed pyroclastic flows. El Chichón (read twice 2026-11-18): Volcano Watch “A holiday visit to exotic El Chichón volcano”, 20 Dec 2012 (usgs.gov/observatories/hvo/news/volcano-watch-a-holiday-visit-exotic-el-chichon-volcano): three explosive eruptions in about a week, nine towns destroyed, more than 2,000 killed and 20,000 homeless, destruction greatest within 10 km (6 mi); volume similar to Mount St. Helens 1980 with about seven times the sulfur dioxide; stratosphere warmed about 4 °C; no large cooling in the following year because of a strong El Niño; new crater 1 km (0.6 mi) wide; last major eruption about 500 years before; “will undoubtedly erupt again”. Galeras, Volcano Watch of 15 Jan 1993 (usgs.gov/news/volcano-watch-galeras-mauna-loa-decade-volcanoes), read 2026-11-17 and 2026-11-21: a small phreatomagmatic explosion in the crater at about 1:40 p.m. on Thursday 14 Jan 1993 killed six volcanologists at a workshop of more than 90 scientists (four from Colombia, one from Great Britain, one from Russia) and three people not attending it; three of the fifteen American participants were injured, one seriously, and one scientist from Ecuador; most of the 33 participants in the group on the rim and inside the crater were gas geochemists standardizing sampling and analysis; a “Decade Volcano” workshop held in Pasto to increase monitoring of Galeras and train volcanologists of Central and South America; Galeras named a Decade Volcano by IAVCEI for its extreme risk, with Mount Rainier and Mauna Loa; more than 400,000 people on its flanks; Pasto the capital of Nariño.
